Happy Thanksgiving to all.
(Thursday puzzle? Didn't see one.)

At a bonfire in college, I told a friend that I was a math major. I remember saying right afterward that I really didn't know why I was drawn to the subject so much.

I can't remember the quote exactly, but my friend said something like this:

"Maybe you know there will be a lot of problems in life you can't solve, but math is this place where you can solve them."

And I thought that was brilliant.

In a way, puzzles give me a similar effervescent feeling: a blank grid just waiting to be filled in and a rush upon reaching the mountaintop. I actually think crosswords, and puzzles in general, are as beautiful as an Impressionist painting or a sun-kissed sky. They draw me in, and I surmise I'm not the only one.

Indeed, puzzles have given me solace throughout the chaos that life so often is. And I love Thanksgiving because, despite this maelstrom, I am thankful. I am thankful for puzzles. I am thankful for random acts of kindness. I am thankful for all of you, for putting up with my puns ("You cooked for me?" "It's the feast I could do!") and for celebrating the brilliant ingenuity of all these constructors and the solvers who love their creations.

To quote Margaret Farrar, "You can't think of your troubles while solving a crossword." She was right. I think instead of the beauty of our language and the interconnected ways in which words can entertain, teach, and even heal.

Wishing you, your family, and your friends the very best of Thanksgivings.

With love,

Mike

I like that the theme answers are in the order of the meal.  I like that the first word of each theme answer has a different meaning in the phrase as usually meant, than in its Thanksgiving meal meaning, for instance, PASSING in “passing remarks” means “transcient”, but in the puzzle it means handing food over.

Very impressive to come up with five such answers that fit the requirements of symmetry!

But mostly, I like the feeling of camaraderie and love emitting from the box today, setting the tone for what is hopefully to follow.  Thank you, Sam and Jeff for brightening my day!

The cluing was great, though.  This is not only the best clue for KALE I've ever seen, but one of the niftiest clues ever.  Loved the clue for NAPES.  And what a cute quote to choose from the ALI collection.

Here are two quotes and a poem:

“It is impossible to be a mathematician without being a poet in soul.” — Sofia Kovalevskaya

“Pure mathematics is, in its way, the poetry of logical ideas.” — Albert Einstein

The mathematicians and physics men
Have their mythology; they work alongside the truth,
Never touching it; their equations are false
But the things work. Or, when gross error appears,
They invent new ones; they drop the theory of waves
In universal ether and imagine curved space.
Nevertheless their equations bombed Hiroshima.
The terrible thing worked.

The poet also
Has his mythology. He tells you the moon arose
Out of the Pacific basin. He tells you that Troy was burnt
for a vagrant
Beautiful woman, her face launched a thousand ships.
It is unlikely: it might be true: but church and state
Depend on more peculiarly impossible myths:
That all men are born free and equal: consider that!*
---------Robinson Jeffers, Late Poems(1953-1962)

Peter, In the NYT XWP, [Government policy kingpin] is always CZAR. The former Russian ruler is TSAR or CZAR (or rarely, noted as a variant, TZAR). CSAR -- which Mrs. Farrar allowed once (by mistake?) in 1961 -- isn't in the dictionary. https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/czar

As @BA said, in the NYT XW, the spelling TSAR--which is a more direct transliteration of the Russian--is almost always reserved for the Russian monarch. CZARs--the "cz" indicates it was filtered through some other Eastern European language, like Polish or Hungarian--is other, non-royal fat cats.

But, lest you feel dim, an article in the November, 1827, issue of *The Asiatic Journal and Monthly Register for British India and Its Dependencies*--which I just happened to have on my bookshelf--tells us that "In order to testify to the conqueror of Siberia his sense of the importance of the services he had rendered his country, the Csar took off his own pelisse, and placed it upon him, in presence of the whole court."
